title: What is Stream.sorted(), and what does "stateful intermediate operation" mean?
shortTitle: Stream.sorted() — stateful intermediate operation, buffers all elements

s1_definition.profdef: `Stream.sorted()` is an intermediate operation that sorts elements by natural order (Comparable) or a custom Comparator. It is STATEFUL because it must BUFFER ALL elements before emitting any — it cannot sort one element without seeing all others first. This contrasts with STATELESS ops like filter and map that process one element at a time (O(1) memory). Stateful ops have implications: (1) O(n) memory (buffer entire stream), (2) BLOCKS FUSION — upstream elements are fully consumed before downstream sees anything, (3) INFINITE STREAMS → hangs forever or OOM (cannot sort infinite data), (4) PARALLEL STREAMS → extra merge overhead.
s1_definition.analogy: Stateless ops (filter, map) are like assembly-line workers — each cheque flows through one at a time. Stateful ops (sorted) are like the sorting machine that says "give me ALL cheques first, then I'll sort them and release them." The machine HOLDS ALL cheques (buffers) before outputting. If cheques keep coming forever (infinite stream), the machine never finishes — it just keeps collecting.
s1_definition.oneliner: sorted() = stateful, buffers ALL elements, O(n) memory, blocks fusion, hangs on infinite streams. filter/map = stateless, one element at a time, O(1).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** `Stream.sorted()` is an intermediate operation that sorts elements by natural order (Comparable) or a custom Comparator. It is STATEFUL because it must BUFFER ALL elements before emitting any — it cannot sort one element without seeing all others first. This contrasts with STATELESS ops like filter and map that process one element at a time (O(1) memory). Stateful ops have implications: (1) O(n) memory (buffer entire stream), (2) BLOCKS FUSION — upstream elements are fully consumed before downstream sees anything, (3) INFINITE STREAMS → hangs forever or OOM (cannot sort infinite data), (4) PARALLEL STREAMS → extra merge overhead.

Other stateful ops: `distinct()` (HashSet of seen elements — O(n)), `limit(n)` and `skip(n)` (counter — O(1) but ordering-dependent in parallel).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Stateless ops (filter, map) are like assembly-line workers — each cheque flows through one at a time. Stateful ops (sorted) are like the sorting machine that says "give me ALL cheques first, then I'll sort them and release them." The machine HOLDS ALL cheques (buffers) before outputting. If cheques keep coming forever (infinite stream), the machine never finishes — it just keeps collecting.

**One line to remember:** sorted() = stateful, buffers ALL elements, O(n) memory, blocks fusion, hangs on infinite streams. filter/map = stateless, one element at a time, O(1).

sections.s3_banking: **Problem — The bank's trade ledger sorts 1 million trades by amount.** The developer placed sorted() before filter(), sorting all 1M trades when only 200K are settled. After profiling, the team reorders: filter first, then sort — 5x speedup. They also demonstrate the fusion-blocking behavior with peek logging and the OOM risk with large unsorted streams.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** 5 symbols: HDFC, RELIANCE, TCS, INFY, WIPRO flow into the pipeline.

**Step 2 — Before sorted().** peek logs each: HDFC, RELIANCE, TCS, INFY, WIPRO. All 5 enter the sorted() buffer.

**Step 3 — sorted() buffers.** Internal array holds all 5. Arrays.sort runs. Order: HDFC, INFY, RELIANCE, TCS, WIPRO.

**Step 4 — After sorted().** Sorted elements emit one-by-one: HDFC→peek→map→collect, INFY→peek→map→collect, etc. Fusion resumes AFTER sorted().

**Step 5 — Optimization.** 100K elements. sort-then-filter: sorts 100K, keeps 20K. filter-then-sort: keeps 20K, sorts 20K. 5x less sorting work.
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ═══ STATEFUL (sorted) vs STATELESS (filter/map) ═══

  STATELESS (filter):
    Element 1 → test → pass/drop → FORGET → Element 2 → test → ...
    Memory: O(1) — one element at a time

  STATEFUL (sorted):
    Element 1 → BUFFER
    Element 2 → BUFFER
    Element 3 → BUFFER
    ...all elements...
    → SORT entire buffer
    → EMIT: sorted[0], sorted[1], sorted[2]...
    Memory: O(n) — entire stream buffered

  ═══ FUSION BLOCKING ═══

  filter → map → sorted → map → collect
    │              │
    │ FUSED        │ FUSION BROKEN
    │ (one pass)   │ (buffer all, then emit)
    ▼              ▼
  [filter+map     [sorted blocks, then map+collect
   per element]    resumes per element]

  ═══ OPTIMIZATION: filter BEFORE sort ═══

  (Avoid) sorted(100K) → filter(→20K)    = sort 100K elements
  (Recommended) filter(→20K) → sorted(20K)     = sort  20K elements  ← 5x faster!
```
sections.s5c_hld:
HLD is the whiteboard overview. In National Bank of India's reporting service, `Stream.sorted()` ranks transactions and accounts (largest transfers, top balances) for the operations dashboard. Because `sorted()` is a stateful intermediate operation, it must buffer all elements before emitting any, so the service streams a bounded page from PostgreSQL, sorts in memory, caches the ranked page in Redis, and never sorts unbounded streams. Heavy ranking jobs run on read replicas; audit events go to Kafka and logs to ELK.

```

  ┌──────────┐ ┌──────────┐
  │ Ops UI   │ │Scheduler │  ← Client Layer
  └────┬─────┘ └────┬─────┘ HTTPS
       └───────┬─────┘
               ▼
        ┌──────────────┐
        │ API Gateway  │  JWT, rate limit
        └──────┬───────┘ REST
               ▼
     ┌──────────────────────┐
     │ Reporting Svc (×3)   │  ← sorted()/comparator ranking
     │  - top transfers     │  buffers bounded page only
     └───┬───────────┬──────┘
   JDBC  │           │ Kafka
         ▼           ▼
  ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐
  │ PostgreSQL   │ │ Kafka audit  │

         ▼           ┌──────────────┐
```

sections.s5d_lld:
LLD shows how sorting is wired as a comparator pipeline and why `sorted()` buffers.

```
  ═══ LLD — Stream.sorted() Ranking ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Strategy: Comparator<Transaction> per sort key            │
  │    WHY: swap ordering without touching pipeline (O/C)     │
  │ Builder:  RankedReport.builder()...build()                │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  ┌─ SOLID Applied ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: RankingService ranks only; repo fetches only           │
  │ O: new sort order = new Comparator, no edit               │
  │ L: any Comparator slots into sorted()                     │
  │ I: small Comparator interface, no fat contract            │
  │ D: service depends on Comparator abstraction              │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──
  ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
  │          RankingService           │
  │  - repo: TransactionRepository    │ ◇
  │  + topTransfers(n): List<Txn>     │
  │  + sortByAmountDesc(): List<Txn>  │
  └──────────────┬────────────────────┘
                 │ uses
                 ▼
  ┌───────────────────────────────────┐
  │   Comparator<Transaction>         │  reversed(), thenComparing()
  └───────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Why sorted() is STATEFUL ──
  source ──filter──▶ [buffer ALL n elements] ──emit sorted──▶ limit(n)
  Cannot emit first element until last is seen → full materialization.

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ──
  1. Controller.topTransfers(5)
  2.  → RankingService.topTransfers(5)
  3.    → repo.findRecentPage(1000)        bounded fetch
  4.    → stream.sorted(byAmount.reversed()) buffers 1000
  5.    → .limit(5)                          emits top 5
  6.    → cache.put(ranked, TTL=30s)
  7.  → return RankedReport
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Stream.sorted is a stateful intermediate operation, meaning it must buffer ALL elements from upstream before producing any output. Unlike stateless operations like filter and map that process one element at a time with O(1) memory, sorted requires O(n) memory to hold the entire stream contents. It blocks fusion: upstream operations are fully consumed into the buffer, the buffer is sorted, and then downstream operations process the sorted elements one at a time.

In my trade ledger service, peek logging proves the buffering behavior: all five "before-sort" entries appear before any "after-sort" entries. The optimization demonstration shows that placing filter before sorted reduces elements to sort by 80% — sorting 20K filtered elements instead of 100K unfiltered elements gives a 5x speedup. This is a critical pipeline ordering rule: always filter, limit, and distinct BEFORE sorted to minimize the buffer size.

The other stateful operations are distinct (maintains an internal HashSet of seen elements — O(n) memory) and limit/skip (maintains a counter — O(1) memory but ordering-aware in parallel). The practical implications: never use sorted on infinite streams (it hangs or throws OOM), and in parallel streams, sorted requires an additional merge-sort step across partitions. For performance-critical code, if you only need the top N elements, consider a priority queue approach or `stream.sorted().limit(n)` — sorted is smart enough to use a partial sort in some implementations.
